title: Import & Organize Your Kit
blurb: Get your own samples onto the unit and lay them out as a kit you can play without hunting for pads.

steps.title: Prepare the files on your computer
body: Trim each sample so it starts exactly on the transient. Silence at the front of a kick is the single most common reason a kit feels late.
Normalize the levels roughly, so a kick and a hat do not arrive twenty decibels apart.
Name the files so they sort in the order you want to place them — a leading number is enough.
Keep them as WAV files. Converting from a lossy format after the fact is work you do not need.
steps.checkpoint: A folder of trimmed, sanely named, roughly level-matched WAVs.
steps.tip: Do this on the computer, where you have a waveform view and undo. Fixing a badly trimmed sample on the unit is possible but slow.

steps.title: Import from the SD card
body: Copy the folder onto the unit's SD card using the import folder the SP-404MKII expects, then put the card back in.
Open the menu and run the import function, then choose the files you want and the pads to place them on.
Import a small batch first — a kick, a snare, and a hat — and confirm they play before moving a hundred files across.
Your firmware's menu wording may differ from the manual you read online. Trust the unit's display over any tutorial.
steps.checkpoint: Three imported samples play from three pads.
steps.tip: Importing does not trim. Whatever you did not fix on the computer, you will now be fixing with START/END on the unit.

steps.title: Lay out the kit deliberately
body: Put the sounds you play most under your strongest fingers: kick, snare, and hat on the bottom row.
Keep the layout the same across every bank you build. A kit you can play blind is worth more than a kit with the perfect sound in the wrong place.
PadLab's 16-pad lessons assume the same idea — pads 1 to 4 are the bottom row — so a consistent layout means the muscle memory carries over.
Leave the top row for the sounds you reach for occasionally: crashes, one-shots, vocal stabs.
steps.checkpoint: You can find kick, snare, and hat without looking at the unit.
steps.tip: Copy the layout of the kit you already practise on. Two different layouts means twice the practice for half the fluency.

steps.title: Trim, level, and label on the unit
body: Play each imported pad and set its start point with START/END so it fires the instant you hit it.
Balance pad levels against each other, not against silence — play the kick and snare alternately while you adjust.
Give each pad a name you will recognize in six months. 'Vox2Final' is not that name.
Save when the bank is how you want it.
steps.checkpoint: Every pad in the bank fires instantly and sits at a sensible level next to its neighbours.
steps.tip: If a pad feels late no matter how you play it, it is almost always the start point rather than your timing.

steps.title: Back it up
body: Copy the project off the SD card to your computer as soon as a kit is worth keeping.
Do it again after any session where you resampled — resampling is destructive, and there is no undo for a pad you overwrote last week.
Keep the source WAVs alongside the backup so you can rebuild the kit from scratch if you need to.
steps.checkpoint: A copy of the project exists somewhere that is not the SD card in the unit.
steps.tip: SD cards fail without warning. The backup takes two minutes; the kit took two hours.
